title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text: How did mathematics produce correct answers from logically incoherent foundations

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
2.1 Newton’s Fluxions
Newton framed calculus in terms of motion. A variable quantity — a “fluent” — flows continuously through time. Its fluxion is its instantaneous rate of flow, the velocity of the quantity. To find the fluxion of \(x^2\), Newton would let \(x\) increase by a small amount \(o\) over a small interval of time, compute the change in \(x^2\), and then divide by \(o\):
\[
\frac{(x + o)^2 - x^2}{o} = \frac{2xo + o^2}{o} = 2x + o
\]
Then Newton would set \(o = 0\) to obtain the fluxion \(2x\).
The result is correct. But the reasoning is not: \(o\) was assumed nonzero to justify the division, then assumed zero to discard the \(o^2/o = o\) term. Both assumptions cannot hold simultaneously.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
2.2 Leibniz’s Differentials
Leibniz developed an equivalent but notationally different approach. He worked with differentials \(dx\) and \(dy\) — infinitely small increments in \(x\) and \(y\). The derivative is the ratio \(dy/dx\). For \(y = x^2\):
\[
dy = (x + dx)^2 - x^2 = 2x\,dx + (dx)^2
\]
Dividing by \(dx\):
\[
\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x + dx
\]
Then \((dx)^2\) and the remaining \(dx\) were dropped as “infinitely small compared to the finite \(2x\),” leaving \(dy/dx = 2x\).
Again: correct answer, incoherent argument. If \(dx \neq 0\), the answer is \(2x + dx\), not \(2x\). If \(dx = 0\), the original division by \(dx\) is illegal.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
2.3 The Pattern
Both methods share the same logical structure:

Introduce a small quantity (\(o\) or \(dx\)) and assume it is nonzero — so division by it is valid.
Expand and simplify.
Discard all remaining powers of the small quantity as negligible.
Obtain the correct answer.

Step 3 is the scandal. The practitioner must decide, by feel, which terms to keep and which to throw away. There is no principled rule — just the implicit understanding that “higher-order infinitesimals are smaller than first-order ones.” What does smaller mean for a quantity that is already infinitely small? Nobody said.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
3.1 The Man and the Motive
George Berkeley (1685–1753), Bishop of Cloyne, was one of the great empiricist philosophers. He had a long-standing grievance with the scientific establishment: mathematicians and natural philosophers had been using their air of precision to attack religious faith, arguing that rigorous rational inquiry had no room for miracles or revelation. Berkeley decided to return the favor.
In 1734 he published The Analyst: A Discourse Addressed to an Infidel Mathematician. His target was almost certainly Edmond Halley (of Halley’s comet fame). His argument was devastating.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
3.2 The Central Critique
Berkeley accepted that the results of calculus were often correct. His attack was on the reasoning. He argued that the logical status of fluxions and infinitesimals was no better — and arguably worse — than the “mysteries” of religion that mathematicians mocked.
His most famous line:

“And what are these Fluxions? The Velocities of evanescent Increments. And what are these same evanescent Increments? They are neither finite Quantities nor Quantities infinitely small, nor yet nothing. May we not call them the Ghosts of departed Quantities?”

The phrase ghosts of departed quantities is one of the most incisive epigrams in the history of science. It captures the problem exactly: the increments are invoked as real quantities when needed for the algebra, then made to vanish when they become inconvenient. They are neither alive (nonzero) nor dead (zero) — they haunt the calculation.
Berkeley further argued that the correct results were obtained not because of the reasoning, but despite it — specifically, because two errors happened to cancel each other out:

“By virtue of a twofold mistake you arrive, though not at science, yet at the truth.”



Berkeley’s deeper philosophical point was that mathematicians demanded clarity in others’ domains (theology) that they conspicuously lacked in their own. The rhetorical force of The Analyst came precisely from this hypocrisy.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
section: 3.3 A Concrete Example of the Double Error
text:
3.3 A Concrete Example of the Double Error
Take the derivative of \(y = x^2\) using the increment method. Berkeley’s “twofold error” argument:

Error 1: Treat \(o\) as nonzero when dividing: \(\frac{(x+o)^2 - x^2}{o} = 2x + o\)
Error 2: Drop the \(o\) term at the end, as if \(o = 0\)

Each step is individually wrong, but the two errors cancel: the first “error” introduces a surplus \(o\), and the second “error” removes exactly that surplus, leaving the correct \(2x\). Berkeley’s point was that this looks like correct reasoning only because of a lucky coincidence in the algebra — and that no general principle justified why it always worked.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
4.1 The Pragmatic Argument
Faced with Berkeley’s critique, most mathematicians responded with something like: the method works; figure out the foundations later. This was not entirely unreasonable. Calculus was producing correct and verifiable predictions about the physical world at a rate that had never been seen before. Abandoning it because of a philosophical objection would have been scientifically catastrophic.
There is a recurring pattern in mathematics where powerful techniques are used for decades or centuries before they are properly understood. (Complex numbers followed a similar arc: routinely used by the 16th century, not rigorously understood until the 19th.)

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
4.2 Attempts at Rigorous Defense
Several mathematicians attempted to answer Berkeley on his own terms:

Colin Maclaurin (Treatise of Fluxions, 1742) tried to recast Newton’s calculus in the language of classical Greek geometry, avoiding infinitesimals entirely. The result was technically defensible but impossibly cumbersome and did not spread.
Jean le Rond d’Alembert argued that the derivative should be understood as a limit — the value approached by the difference quotient as the increment tends to zero. This was the germ of the right idea, but d’Alembert had no rigorous definition of “limit” and no way to make the argument precise.
Leonhard Euler simply treated infinitesimals as exactly zero when convenient. His results were almost always correct (Euler had preternatural instincts), but his justification satisfied no one who was paying attention.

None of these responses answered Berkeley rigorously. The foundations remained contested.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
5.1 Cauchy’s Reconstruction
The decisive step was taken by Augustin-Louis Cauchy in his Cours d’analyse (1821). Cauchy systematically rebuilt calculus on the concept of a limit, defined informally as follows:

A variable quantity \(u_n\) has limit \(\ell\) if, for any desired precision, the values of \(u_n\) eventually stay within that precision of \(\ell\).

He defined the derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) as:
\[
f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
\]
The key move: \(h\) never equals zero in this definition. The limit describes the behavior of the difference quotient as \(h\) approaches zero, not at \(h = 0\). No quantity is ever simultaneously nonzero and zero. The ghost is exorcised.
Cauchy also gave the first rigorous definitions of continuity and of the definite integral (as the limit of Riemann sums), constructing the whole edifice from the limit concept upward.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
5.2 Weierstrass’s Formalization
Cauchy’s limits still relied on intuitive language (“approaches,” “eventually”). Karl Weierstrass (1815–1897) replaced this with purely logical, quantifier-based definitions — eliminating all appeal to motion or intuition.
The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition of a limit:
\[
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L
\quad \iff \quad
\forall\, \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists\, \delta > 0 \text{ such that } 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon
\]


The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition replaced vague words like “approaches” with hard inequalities. It turned the limit from a dynamic process into a static logical statement — one that can be verified or refuted without any reference to time, motion, or “infinitely small” quantities.
This definition contains no infinitesimals, no motion, no intuition. Every term is a real number; every statement is a logical condition. With this, the derivative is:
\[
f'(a) = L \iff \forall\,\varepsilon > 0,\; \exists\,\delta > 0 \text{ such that } 0 < |h| < \delta \implies \left|\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} - L\right| < \varepsilon
\]
For \(f(x) = x^2\), \(a = x\):
\[
\left|\frac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h} - 2x\right| = \left|2x + h - 2x\right| = |h|
\]
So for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), choose \(\delta = \varepsilon\). Then \(0 < |h| < \delta\) implies \(|h| < \varepsilon\). The limit is \(2x\), rigorously. No ghosts anywhere.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
5.3 What Changed








Era
Foundation
Status of \(dx\)




Newton / Leibniz
Fluxions / differentials
Nonzero then zero — inconsistent


Cauchy (1821)
Limits (intuitive)
Eliminated; limit is about approach, not arrival


Weierstrass (1860s)
\(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\)
Eliminated; purely static logical condition



The 150-year crisis was resolved by changing the question. Instead of asking “what is an infinitely small quantity?”, Weierstrass asked “when does a function’s value get arbitrarily close to a target?” The second question has a precise answer that requires no new ontology.

title: The Foundational Crisis of Calculus
text:
6.1 Non-Standard Analysis
The story has a surprising coda. In 1960, logician Abraham Robinson proved that it is possible to extend the real numbers to a larger ordered field — the hyperreals — that genuinely contains infinitely small (and infinitely large) elements, and that this extension is logically consistent (assuming standard set theory is consistent).
In Robinson’s non-standard analysis, \(dx\) is a genuine nonzero infinitesimal, and \(dy/dx = 2x\) follows rigorously without epsilon-delta arguments. The intuitions of Newton and Leibniz were, in a deep sense, vindicated: infinitesimals can be made rigorous. Berkeley’s objection was not that infinitesimals were the wrong idea, but that they had not been defined properly.


Robinson’s hyperreals satisfy the transfer principle: any first-order statement true of the reals is also true of the hyperreals. This is what makes non-standard analysis consistent — it is not a different mathematics, but an extension of the same one.
The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) approach and non-standard analysis give identical results. They are two different foundations for the same edifice. Today, \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) dominates in university courses, largely for historical and pedagogical reasons — not because infinitesimals are wrong, but because Weierstrass got there first.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text: Based on David Romer, “Advanced Macroeconomics,” 3rd edition, Chapter 1.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
2.1 The Three Inputs
The economy produces a single good \(Y\) using three inputs:

Capital \(K(t)\): the stock of physical capital (machines, structures, equipment).
Labor \(L(t)\): the number of workers.
Technology \(A(t)\): the level of productive knowledge.

All variables are continuous functions of time \(t\).

title: The Solow Growth Model
section: 2.2 Exogenous Growth of Labor and Technology
text:
2.2 Exogenous Growth of Labor and Technology
Both \(L\) and \(A\) grow at constant, exogenous rates:
\[
\dot{L}(t) = n \, L(t)
\tag{1}\]
\[
\dot{A}(t) = g \, A(t)
\tag{2}\]


Notation
\(\dot{x} \equiv dx/dt\) is the time derivative of \(x\).
\(n\) = population (labor) growth rate. Typical value: 1–2% per year.
\(g\) = rate of labor-augmenting technological progress. Typical value: 1–2% per year.
Integrating Equation 1 and Equation 2:
\[
L(t) = L(0)\,e^{nt}, \qquad A(t) = A(0)\,e^{gt}
\]
Economic intuition: Population growth is treated as a pure demographic fact — exogenous to the model. Technological progress reflects cumulative human knowledge, also treated as exogenous here. This exogeneity is the model’s key limitation and the starting point for endogenous growth theory.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
2.3 The Production Function
Output is:
\[
Y(t) = F\!\bigl(K(t),\; A(t)\,L(t)\bigr)
\tag{3}\]


Notation
\(Y\) = aggregate output (GDP).
\(K\) = aggregate capital stock.
\(A(t)L(t)\) = “effective labor.” One worker with technology \(A\) is as productive as \(A\) workers at baseline technology.
This specification of technology as labor-augmenting (also called Harrod-neutral) is necessary for a balanced growth path to exist.

2.3.1 Assumption 1 — Constant Returns to Scale
For any scalar \(c > 0\):
\[
F(cK,\; cAL) = c\,F(K,\;AL)
\tag{4}\]
Doubling all inputs exactly doubles output. The standard justification is replication: clone a factory together with all its workers, and output doubles.


2.3.2 Assumption 2 — Positive, Diminishing Marginal Products
\[
F_K > 0,\quad F_{AL} > 0; \qquad F_{KK} < 0,\quad F_{AL,AL} < 0
\tag{5}\]
More capital or more effective labor raises output, but at a declining rate. The first machine is very productive; the hundredth less so because it competes for the same workers.


2.3.3 Assumption 3 — Inada Conditions
\[
\lim_{K \to 0} F_K = \infty,\quad \lim_{K \to \infty} F_K = 0
\tag{6}\]
\[
\lim_{AL \to 0} F_{AL} = \infty,\quad \lim_{AL \to \infty} F_{AL} = 0
\tag{7}\]


Inada conditions guarantee that the \(sf(k)\) curve starts above the break-even line near \(k=0\) and falls below it for large \(k\), ensuring a unique interior steady state. Named after Ken-Ichi Inada (1963).
When capital is scarce, an additional unit is enormously valuable (infinite marginal product). When capital is abundant, extra units add almost nothing. These two boundary conditions, combined with continuity, pin down a unique positive steady state.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
2.4 Capital Accumulation


Notation
\(s\) = saving rate, \(s \in (0,1)\). The fraction of output households save. Treated as exogenous and constant in the Solow model.
\(\delta\) = depreciation rate of capital. Typical value: 5–10% per year.
A fixed fraction \(s\) of output is saved and invested:
\[
\dot{K}(t) = s\,Y(t) - \delta\,K(t)
\tag{8}\]
The capital stock rises by gross investment \(sY\) and falls by depreciation \(\delta K\).

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
3.1 Transforming Variables
Working in levels is cumbersome because \(K\), \(L\), and \(A\) all trend upward. Instead, divide by \(A(t)L(t)\) — the total number of effective workers — to obtain stationary variables:
\[
k(t) \;\equiv\; \frac{K(t)}{A(t)\,L(t)}, \qquad y(t) \;\equiv\; \frac{Y(t)}{A(t)\,L(t)}
\tag{9}\]


Notation
\(k\) = capital per effective worker.
\(y\) = output per effective worker.
Dividing by \(AL\) (not just \(L\)) removes both population growth and technological growth, leaving a variable that is constant in the long run.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
3.2 Intensive-Form Production Function
Apply the CRS property (Equation 4) with \(c = 1/(AL)\):
\[
F\!\left(\frac{K}{AL},\;1\right) = \frac{1}{AL}\,F(K,\,AL) = \frac{Y}{AL} = y
\]
So we can write:
\[
y = f(k), \qquad \text{where } f(k) \equiv F(k,\,1)
\tag{10}\]
The intensive-form function \(f\) inherits the properties of \(F\): \(f'>0\), \(f''<0\), \(f(0)=0\), with Inada conditions \(f'(0)=\infty\) and \(f'(\infty)=0\).

Cobb-Douglas example. If \(F(K,AL)=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), then \[f(k)=k^\alpha \tag{11}\] This is the most common functional form in applications.

title: The Solow Growth Model
section: 3.3 Deriving the Equation of Motion for \(k\)
text:
3.3 Deriving the Equation of Motion for \(k\)
Differentiate the definition \(k = K/(AL)\) with respect to time (quotient rule):
\[
\dot{k} = \frac{\dot{K}}{AL} - \frac{K}{AL}\cdot\frac{d(AL)/dt}{AL}
\]
The growth rate of \(AL\) is:
\[
\frac{d(AL)/dt}{AL} = \frac{\dot{A}L + A\dot{L}}{AL} = \frac{\dot{A}}{A} + \frac{\dot{L}}{L} = g + n
\]
So:
\[
\dot{k} = \frac{\dot{K}}{AL} - (n+g)\,k
\tag{12}\]
Substitute \(\dot{K} = sY - \delta K\) from Equation 8:
\[
\dot{k} = \frac{sY - \delta K}{AL} - (n+g)\,k = s\cdot\frac{Y}{AL} - \delta\cdot\frac{K}{AL} - (n+g)\,k
\]
Using Equation 9 and Equation 10:
\[
\boxed{\dot{k} = s\,f(k) - (n + g + \delta)\,k}
\tag{13}\]


Equation 13 is the engine of the Solow model. It fully describes how the economy evolves over time. All the model’s predictions — the steady state, convergence, comparative statics — follow directly from this single equation.
Term-by-term intuition for Equation 13:







Term
Meaning




\(s\,f(k)\)
Actual investment per effective worker: the fraction \(s\) of output that gets saved and added to capital


\(\delta\, k\)
Capital lost to depreciation


\(n\,k\)
Capital diluted by new workers joining the labor force


\(g\,k\)
Capital diluted because each worker becomes more productive (the same \(K\) now serves a larger effective workforce)


\((n+g+\delta)k\)
Total break-even investment: what must be invested just to keep \(k\) constant



\(k\) rises when actual investment exceeds break-even, and falls otherwise.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
4.1 Existence and Uniqueness
A steady state is a value \(k^*>0\) at which \(\dot{k}=0\). Setting Equation 13 to zero:
\[
s\,f(k^*) = (n+g+\delta)\,k^*
\tag{14}\]


The steady state \(k^*\) depends on \(s\), \(n\), \(g\), and \(\delta\). A country with a higher saving rate or lower population growth has a higher \(k^*\) and therefore a higher long-run standard of living.
Existence and uniqueness via Inada conditions. Define \(h(k) \equiv sf(k)/[(n+g+\delta)k] = sf(k)/k \cdot 1/(n+g+\delta)\). By the Inada conditions:
\[
\lim_{k\to 0} h(k) = \frac{s \cdot f'(0)}{n+g+\delta} = \infty, \qquad \lim_{k\to\infty} h(k) = \frac{s\cdot 0}{n+g+\delta} = 0
\]
Because \(h\) is continuous and strictly decreasing (since \(f''<0\)), there is exactly one \(k^*>0\) where \(h(k^*)=1\), i.e., where the two curves cross.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
4.2 Stability
For \(k < k^*\): \(sf(k) > (n+g+\delta)k\) so \(\dot{k}>0\) (capital accumulates). For \(k > k^*\): \(sf(k) < (n+g+\delta)k\) so \(\dot{k}<0\) (capital decumulates).
Therefore \(k^*\) is globally stable: any economy starting at \(k(0)>0\) converges to \(k^*\).

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
4.3 Long-Run Growth Rates
Once the economy reaches \(k^*\), what grows and at what rate?



Variable
Definition
Growth rate at \(k^*\)




\(k = K/(AL)\)
Capital per effective worker
0


\(y = Y/(AL)\)
Output per effective worker
0


\(K/L\)
Capital per worker
\(g\)


\(Y/L\)
Output per worker (living standard)
\(g\)


\(Y\)
Total output
\(n+g\)





The central prediction: In the long run, output per worker grows at rate \(g\) — the rate of technology — regardless of the saving rate \(s\). Saving affects the level of output per worker, not its long-run growth rate.
Key insight. The saving rate \(s\) has no effect on the long-run growth rate of per-capita income. It only affects the level. This sharp prediction distinguishes the Solow model from models with linear production functions (AK models), where \(s\) permanently raises the growth rate.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
5.1 Speed of Convergence
How fast does the economy approach \(k^*\)? Define the deviation \(\tilde{k}(t) \equiv k(t) - k^*\). Linearizing \(\dot{k} = \phi(k) \equiv sf(k)-(n+g+\delta)k\) around \(k^*\):
\[
\dot{\tilde{k}} \approx \phi'(k^*)\,\tilde{k}
\tag{15}\]
where
\[
\phi'(k^*) = sf'(k^*) - (n+g+\delta)
\tag{16}\]
Equation 15 is just a first-order linear ODE with constant coefficient \(\phi'(k^*)\). Separating variables and integrating:
\[
\frac{d\tilde{k}}{\tilde{k}} = \phi'(k^*)\,dt
\;\implies\;
\ln \tilde{k}(t) = \phi'(k^*)\,t + C
\;\implies\;
\tilde{k}(t) = \tilde{k}(0)\,e^{\phi'(k^*)\,t}
\]
At a stable steady state, \(\phi'(k^*) < 0\) (the curve \(\dot{k}\) slopes downward at \(k^*\)), so this solution decays to zero — the economy returns to \(k^*\). We define \(\lambda\) simply to replace the negative coefficient with a positive one:
\[
\lambda \;\equiv\; -\phi'(k^*) > 0
\]
so the solution reads more naturally as exponential decay:
\[
\tilde{k}(t) \approx \tilde{k}(0)\,e^{-\lambda t}
\tag{17}\]


\(\lambda > 0\) is the convergence rate: the fraction of the remaining gap closed per unit time. A larger \(\lambda\) means faster convergence.
It remains to compute \(\lambda\) explicitly. Define \(\alpha_K^* \equiv k^*f'(k^*)/f(k^*)\) as the capital share at the steady state. The steady-state condition \(sf(k^*) = (n+g+\delta)k^*\) implies:
\[
s = \frac{(n+g+\delta)\,k^*}{f(k^*)}
\tag{18}\]
Substituting into \(\lambda = (n+g+\delta) - sf'(k^*)\):
\[
\lambda = (n+g+\delta) - \frac{(n+g+\delta)\,k^*}{f(k^*)}\cdot f'(k^*)
= (n+g+\delta)\!\left(1 - \frac{k^*f'(k^*)}{f(k^*)}\right)
= (n+g+\delta)\bigl(1 - \alpha_K^*\bigr)
\tag{19}\]
The economy closes a fraction \(1-e^{-\lambda t}\) of the gap each period.
Numerical example. With \(\alpha_K^* = 1/3\), \(n=0.01\), \(g=0.02\), \(\delta=0.05\):
\[
\lambda = (0.01+0.02+0.05)\bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{3}\bigr) = 0.08 \times \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 5.3\%
\]
Half-life \(= \ln 2 / \lambda \approx 13\) years. If human capital is included and \(\alpha_K^* \approx 2/3\), then \(\lambda \approx 2.7\%\) and the half-life is about 26 years, which matches cross-country empirical estimates better.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
5.2 Absolute vs. Conditional Convergence

Absolute convergence: all countries converge to the same \(k^*\). Requires identical \(s\), \(n\), \(g\), \(\delta\), and technology — unrealistic.
Conditional convergence: each country converges to its own \(k^*\) determined by its parameters. Countries below their own steady state grow faster. This is what cross-country data support: controlling for steady-state determinants, poorer countries grow faster.

title: The Solow Growth Model
section: 6.1 A Rise in the Saving Rate \(s\)
text:
6.1 A Rise in the Saving Rate \(s\)
Suppose \(s\) rises permanently from \(s_1\) to \(s_2 > s_1\).
Step 1. The break-even line \((n+g+\delta)k\) is unchanged. The actual investment curve shifts up. A new (higher) steady state \(k_2^* > k_1^*\) emerges from Equation 14.
Step 2. At the moment of the shock, \(k = k_1^*\) but \(s_2 f(k_1^*) > (n+g+\delta)k_1^*\), so \(\dot{k} > 0\) and capital accumulation resumes.
Step 3. Output per effective worker rises from \(y_1^* = f(k_1^*)\) to \(y_2^* = f(k_2^*) > y_1^*\).
Step 4. The long-run growth rate of \(Y/L\) remains \(g\) — higher \(s\) only raises the level.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
6.2 A Rise in Population Growth \(n\)
A higher \(n\) steepens the break-even line. The actual investment curve \(sf(k)\) is unchanged, so the intersection moves to the left: \(k^{**} < k^*\).
\[
(n_2 + g + \delta)k^{**} = sf(k^{**}), \quad n_2 > n_1 \implies k^{**} < k^*
\tag{20}\]
Higher population growth lowers steady-state capital and output per effective worker. The model predicts a negative cross-country correlation between \(n\) and per-capita income, consistent with the data.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
7.1 Maximizing Steady-State Consumption
The steady state \(k^*\) is pinned down by \(s\), but which steady state maximizes consumption per effective worker? Steady-state consumption is:
\[
c^* = y^* - i^* = f(k^*) - sf(k^*)
\tag{21}\]
Using Equation 14, \(sf(k^*) = (n+g+\delta)k^*\), so:
\[
c^* = f(k^*) - (n+g+\delta)\,k^*
\tag{22}\]


Equation 22 has a clean geometric interpretation: \(c^*\) is the vertical gap between the production function \(f(k^*)\) and the break-even line \((n+g+\delta)k^*\). Maximizing \(c^*\) is equivalent to maximizing this gap.
To maximize \(c^*\) over \(k^*\), differentiate with respect to \(k^*\) and set to zero:
\[
\frac{dc^*}{dk^*} = f'(k^*) - (n+g+\delta) = 0
\]
\[
\boxed{f'(k_{\text{gold}}) = n + g + \delta}
\tag{23}\]
This is the Golden Rule of capital accumulation. The optimal long-run capital stock equates the marginal product of capital to the effective depreciation rate.
Economic intuition. Investing one more unit of capital raises output by \(f'(k)\) but costs \((n+g+\delta)\) per period to maintain (depreciation plus dilution from growth). At the Golden Rule, these exactly balance. Below \(k_\text{gold}\), the return exceeds the cost — invest more. Above \(k_\text{gold}\), the cost exceeds the return — invest less.

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
7.2 The Golden Rule Saving Rate
The Golden Rule saving rate \(s_\text{gold}\) is the value of \(s\) that makes the model’s steady state equal to \(k_\text{gold}\). Using Equation 14 at \(k_\text{gold}\):
\[
s_\text{gold} = \frac{(n+g+\delta)\,k_\text{gold}}{f(k_\text{gold})}
\tag{24}\]
For Cobb-Douglas (Equation 11), \(f'(k)=\alpha k^{\alpha-1}\), so Equation 23 gives \(\alpha k_\text{gold}^{\alpha-1} = n+g+\delta\). Using this in Equation 24:
\[
s_\text{gold} = \frac{f'(k_\text{gold})\,k_\text{gold}}{f(k_\text{gold})} = \frac{\alpha\,k_\text{gold}^\alpha}{k_\text{gold}^\alpha} = \alpha
\]
A remarkable result: for Cobb-Douglas, the Golden Rule saving rate equals the capital share \(\alpha\). If \(\alpha \approx 1/3\), then \(s_\text{gold} \approx 33\%\).

title: The Solow Growth Model
text:
7.3 Dynamic Inefficiency
Compare the economy’s actual steady state \(k^*\) to the Golden Rule \(k_\text{gold}\):

\(k^* < k_\text{gold}\) (under-accumulation): Raising \(s\) increases \(k^*\) toward \(k_\text{gold}\) and eventually raises consumption. But there is a short-run cost — higher saving means less consumption today. This is a genuine intertemporal trade-off.
\(k^* > k_\text{gold}\) (over-accumulation, dynamic inefficiency): Reducing \(s\) raises consumption immediately and permanently — a true free lunch. No one needs to sacrifice. Empirical evidence suggests most countries have \(k^* < k_\text{gold}\), so dynamic inefficiency is not a practical concern for the Solow model.
